name: CPU

claims.claim_text: Not every workload needs full arithmetic precision from a processor. Image compression, video playback and streaming tolerate small computational errors invisibly, so full-width floating-point precision spends processor energy on accuracy the output cannot show, whereas scientific simulation is precision-critical.
claims.quote_verbatim: But when you're doing visual compression, visual playback and streaming and video stuff, you can have errors in your CPU and it does not matter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Back Into The Swing Of Things

claims.claim_text: RISC stands for reduced instruction set computer, a term dating from the 1980s. An open processor project of this kind is distributed not as silicon but as a complete design in a hardware description language such as VHDL or Verilog, which anyone can synthesise.
claims.quote_verbatim: risk being, you know, reduced instruction set computer, right? CPU. Nice 80s term.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Alteritous Andy's Absquatulation

claims.claim_text: Processor selection for a consumer product is normally a commercial decision rather than a technical one: the chumby used a Marvell applications processor originally built for smart photo frames and media tablets because the cost-performance and the price were right and the feature set was adequate.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were looking for an outstanding CPU with, you know, really good cost performance. And, um, you know, one of their, you know, one of their sales guys came down and had a conversation. The price was right. Um, features look good
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Marvell does not sell its processors as an open-market catalogue part; it works vertical by vertical, pursuing named design wins directly rather than serving general distribution.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're not sort of an open market provider. They go for verticals.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: The common belief that FPGAs are priced far above other silicon does not hold at the level of vendor economics: FPGA and processor makers price on substantially the same model, and the gross margins of Xilinx and Intel sit within a few percent of each other.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're priced pretty much with the same model. If you look at the gross margin for Xilinx versus, say, gross margin for Intel, they're within a few percent of each other.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Time-critical signal-processing routines are sometimes hand-written in assembly rather than a high-level language, because the compiler's code generation is not predictable enough at the cycle level and the author needs direct control over what the processor executes.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't trust, I don't know what that compiler is going to make if I write high-level code. This is going to be time-critical, high-speed optimized code doing signal processing. I need to be in control of the CPU.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Intel's processor architectures were cloned far more widely than any other vendor's because Intel treated them as standard products it did not defend once they reached end of life: the 8080 begat the Z80, the PC line was reimplemented by AMD, Cyrix and IBM, and the 8051 and 8048 were second-sourced by hundreds of companies. Microcontroller vendors took the opposite line, so there is no knockoff 6809, PIC or AVR.
claims.quote_verbatim: You do not find a knockoff 6802 or a knockoff 6809. Only Motorola made that. You don't find a knockoff pick. You don't find a knockoff AVR. You don't find a knockoff whatever. But you do find knockoffs of every single bloody chip Intel has ever made. Whether it's... Whether it's... I mean, the 8000... The 8080 became the Z80. The whole PC line has been cloned by AMD, Zyrex, IBM
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: A vendor whose business rests on a single proprietary core will not license it for a compatible clone at any price; the licensing conversation ends with questions about who the customer is, because a second source would compete directly with the only product the vendor sells.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're going to make a knockoff of my CPU? Weird selling guy. Yeah. You're going to... What's that chip for? Oh, who's your customer? Let me talk to your customer here. And you are going to go out of business. These guys, these guys do not... They don't want to have any other players
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Optimising numerical code close to the processor can be framed as an energy problem rather than a timing one: given the input data and the required output bit pattern, the goal is the instruction sequence that moves the least charge through the processor to reach that pattern.
claims.quote_verbatim: I look at the input data. I look at the output bit pattern I want. I figure out what's the least amount – what instructions can I execute to pump the least amount of charge through that CPU to get that final bit pattern.
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: The signal-processing throughput of a general-purpose desktop processor is high enough that a software-defined radio can stream samples to a host PC and omit an FPGA entirely, trading board complexity and FPGA development time for dependence on the host's compute.
claims.quote_verbatim: modern PC CPUs are just incredible in their, in their ability to do signal processing. So, uh, based on that availability of, of that power that people can plug in, uh, I, I thought, uh, let's just see how it goes without an FPGA.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Offloading a workload to a GPU is not automatically faster than running it on the processor: for a particular video codec, source format and driver stack, an overclocked desktop processor running at around three and a half gigahertz beat the discrete graphics card, and the OpenCL and CUDA paths behave as different systems rather than interchangeable ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still not faster than my CPU at rendering my particular video in my particular case with my particular codec, with my particular source files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: Falling back from hardware-accelerated encoding to the processor is not a marginal penalty: encoding at 50 to 60 frames per second on the processor alone ran roughly six times slower than the accelerated path.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm just going back to using my CPU and just, well, if I want to do 50, 60 frames per second, eh, I've got to cop it. Six times slower.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prepping For Hoverboards - Gallionic GitHub Gabble

claims.claim_text: The basic organisation of a processor has not changed: data is moved from one register to the next along a pipeline of transistor stages. What modern parts add is depth and breadth, running several pipelines in parallel rather than a single one.
claims.quote_verbatim: Data moves from one register to the next and, you know, through the pipeline. But now they're heavily, you know, multi-pipeline
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Old Books, New Tricks - Iterant Inscription Irrationality

claims.claim_text: Repurposing a high-volume tablet applications processor for an embedded task inherits both the compute and the analogue plumbing: because tablets need them, the part already carries audio input and output alongside an ARM Cortex-A8 core, and the tablet volumes keep it low-power and inexpensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's initially designed for tablets. So it has a whole CPU in there, you know? So first of all, and then second, it also has audio input and audio output because tablets usually have that. Yeah. And that makes it very, very convenient, uh, to use. So it's low, it's low power. It's, it's fairly inexpensive
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland of Audeme

claims.claim_text: A processor paired with an FPGA typically talks to it over two separate paths: wide streaming links carrying the payload, in this case two 24-bit RGB streams, and a narrow general-purpose parallel memory bus, here a 16-bit GPMC, that exists only so the processor can read and write control registers inside the FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a GPMC bus, which is basically just a 16-bit parallel bus that you use to access registers in the FPGA. So the CPU can control settings in the FPGA.
claims.speaker: David Kronstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: An exposed debug header is a control interface, not just a diagnostic one. A ten-pin ARM JTAG connector reachable through an expansion-module opening on an industrial controller allowed a small microcontroller board, powered from the connector itself, to halt the processor and write a GPIO to change an output within seconds of being plugged in.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can see a 10 pin arm JTAG header. So what I did is I, I made a little device, I plugged a little Arduino in it and I had a script so when I plug that in, it gets power from the connector. It turns on, it waits five seconds, it halts the CPU and writes to a GPIO to turn off your output.
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe FitzPatrick

claims.claim_text: Buying one sample of a target industrial controller establishes the processor and base firmware for every unit of that model, so an attacker who gains JTAG control and reverse-engineers which GPIOs drive which outputs can manipulate the machine without ever extracting or analysing the firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know exactly what CPU is inside. I can assume anything, the same model is going to have the same CPU, um, and the same base firmware. I didn't actually poke at the firmware at all.
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe FitzPatrick

claims.claim_text: Early machines without a dedicated display processor generated video from the processor itself, taking an interrupt on every scan line to pull pixels out of memory and push them to the display; the result could consume roughly half of the machine's total processor throughput before any application work was done.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was no display processor. It was actually the CPU that was doing this. Ah. Right, yeah. So every scan line in the CPU was basically interrupted pulling pixels out of memory and sending them to display. So you could end up having like half of your CPU just used for putting pixels on the screen.
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: Console-era graphics hardware existed because the processor could not afford the work: a Super Nintendo ran a 16-bit processor at only a few megahertz, and a naive frame buffer where every byte of memory maps to a pixel demands both a large amount of RAM and enough processor throughput to write every pixel every frame.
claims.quote_verbatim: a 16-bit CPU that runs at 3-point spare change megahertz. Really? I didn't know that. So, if you have graphics done the, like, in a naive way, but just having a frame buffer, like every single byte in memory equals a pixel in RAM, then first of all, you need a fair amount of RAM, at least at that time, and secondly, you need a fair amount of CPU power in order to push all those pixels
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: The practical value of RISC-V is legal rather than technical: processor cores were downloadable from repositories such as opencores.org long before it existed, but using one in a product that grew large exposed the user to claims from the architecture's owner, whereas an open instruction set carries no such encumbrance.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was really hard to get an IP that was unencumbered by, if I use this in a product that grows anywhere near big, then I will have Intel or ARM or whatever
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: The hidden cost of building around a one-off instruction set is toolchain maintenance rather than the core itself: a well-written core from a single author typically comes with a compiler fork that was never merged upstream and has not been updated in years, which is why designers otherwise fell back on antique architectures such as the Z80 or 8051 whose toolchains are already maintained.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were made by one random guy who also developed the ISA and there is a GCC, you know, fork that never has been mainlined, that has been updated like 10 years ago
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Writing hardware description in a general-purpose programming language turns a core into a generator: a parameterised RISC-V implementation such as VexRiscv exposes options for a memory management unit, floating point or vector support, and emits a different processor depending on which are selected.
claims.quote_verbatim: an amazing implementation of risk five. And when you get the project, you can turn on and off all these different parameters. Do you want a memory management unit? Do you want floating point? Do you want vector? And it generates a whole different CPU depending on what parameters you put in.
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: A two-dimensional graphics accelerator removes blitting work from the processor by consuming a command list already in memory: the processor writes a list of draw operations with position and transparency, and the hardware walks the list, fetches the source data and writes the frame buffer, operating on eight pixels per step instead of one.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of the CPU having to copy all this memory around to draw graphics to the screen, I create some hardware that you feed it a command list. So draw this graphic at this position on the screen and with this color being transparent and it's a list of these in memory. And then the hardware goes through that list in memory and fetches that memory and draws it to the destination, like the frame buffer for the screen. And because it's in hardware, I can do things like operate on eight pixels at a time
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: The general-purpose processor is no longer the default engine for demanding workloads. Over roughly the last decade the pattern shifted toward application-specific hardware, GPUs and ASICs, which cost more to build but are faster and more energy-efficient at the task they were designed for.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is the way it was until maybe 10 years ago. Now you're getting a lot more of those application specific hardware, right? So the classic CPU that you always use for everything is not really the way it's done anymore
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello
claims.episode_title: Quantum Computing with Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: A processor newer than the motherboard firmware that has to start it will not boot, and the board's diagnostic indicators can point at the wrong subsystem: a DRAM error LED lit while the actual fault was an unsupported processor, sending the owner after memory and memory timing instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's something wrong with the memory and the memory timing. It was Intel memory. So I'm trying to figure out, you know, like, is it the bloody, you know, it must be the DRAM, right? Because this motherboard supports the CPU. No, no. It turns out it's the CPU apparently.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Thousands Of Dependencies

claims.claim_text: Because a board cannot flash the firmware that would support a new processor without first booting on some processor, AMD runs a loan programme that ships an older compatible part to the customer, who fits it, updates the firmware, and returns the loaner.
claims.quote_verbatim: AMD actually have this program where they loan out old CPUs. If you contact them, they will actually, yeah, they will ship you an old CPU so that you can put it in their socket so you can upgrade the firmware and then you ship it back to them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Thousands Of Dependencies

claims.claim_text: A simple processor is not a separate category of design from the building blocks beneath it: once a full adder and a state machine have been built, the datapath and the control that sequences it are most of what a rudimentary processor is.
claims.quote_verbatim: after you've built a full adder and a state machine, you're like, you're halfway there to a very simple CPU
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: A standardised compute-module footprint decouples the processor from the carrier board: an industrial design can drop in a faster module years later against the same pinout and the same operating system layer, retesting rather than redesigning. The cost of the modularity is paying for interfaces the product does not use.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the SIP footprint stays the same, if we have a flexible system that Linux provides, then we can just target the same pinouts to this SIP footprint, same functionality. Obviously, I have to test it as the board designer, but I then benefit from better technology, basically. Absolutely. The modular approach is just great. I mean, of course, it also has some insights. You're always paying for interfaces that you wouldn't necessarily need
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: The cache hierarchy exists to minimise the cost of moving data, and it works because general-purpose code has strong spatial and temporal locality: data used in a computation is very likely to be used again shortly within the same program context, so keeping it close pays for itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason you have this hierarchy is because you're trying to minimize the cost of moving memory around and generally in the CPU you've got pretty good locality. So spatial and temporal locality. What that means is you're computing a value and you're using some data. The probability that you're going to be reusing that data within the same program context pretty soon is really, really high. And so you can utilize that to say, hey, we're just like keep the data around and that way once you need the data you don't have to get it from that far away
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Machine-learning accelerators break the assumption the cache hierarchy is built on. Weights are reused and can be held in place, but incoming activation data is consumed once and discarded, so there is little reuse to exploit and the memory design has to be reasoned about differently from a processor's.
claims.quote_verbatim: The weights you reuse, the weights you can like keep in place, but the data actually gets used pretty quickly and then discarded and you can't like reuse it that much
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Load-to-use latency is one of the strongest single predictors of processor performance: the number of cycles it takes to return a value from the L1 cache to the core is highly correlated with delivered performance, and the difference between a three-cycle and a four-cycle L1 is substantial.
claims.quote_verbatim: how quickly you can get a load value back to the core is one of the best predictors, or is a very, very good predictor of your performance. So it's highly correlated. So let's say I do a load. If my minimum time to get the data back from my L1 cache is three cycles or four cycles is going to make a massive difference
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: A processor is general-purpose hardware defined by the obligation to execute anyone's code reasonably well, which is a different design problem from executing one known workload as fast as possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: CPU is a general purpose hardware. It needs to take pretty much everyone's code and execute it pretty well
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Embedded processor cores are designed against two hard constraints beyond performance: a power envelope set by the battery life of the end device, and core area, because die area translates directly into manufacturing cost and therefore into the price of the chip and the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: not only the power envelope, because you don't want someone's battery to, phone battery to instantly die. So you need to keep the power consumption kind of under wraps, but you also have area constraints because how big you make your CPU cores is going to directly translate into manufacturing costs. And so the cost of the chip and the cost of the device
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: An architecture licence is a conformance contract, not a starting point: a core declared to implement a given revision of the ARM architecture must implement the features that revision specifies and perform acceptably on them, which bounds how far an implementer can specialise.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we have a contract which is going to say, hey, this is going to run the ARM architecture v9.something and it's going to have all these features and you need to implement these features and make them so that this is going to be pretty well performant for most of the users out there
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: The trade for abandoning general-purpose design is stark. A specialised chip built for one known use case, with no obligation to legacy or even to general code, can be made very fast, but it is expensive to build, full of custom parts, hard for anyone else to program, and useless outside its target task.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can build a specialized chip for it. And the analogy here would be you're making a Formula One car. It's going to do your thing really, really fast. It's going to be super expensive to build. It's going to have lots of custom parts. No one's going to know how to drive it. The turning radius is going to be awful and it's absolutely not street legal
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: The hardware that happens to be available shapes which algorithms are pursued: the network architectures treated as state of the art in machine learning were selected in part because they run well on existing hardware rather than because they are the best available approach.
claims.quote_verbatim: how much the underlying hardware shapes what we do with it. So say, for example, I'm not an AI fangirl, but I'm going to use AI for this example. How much of what is currently the state-of-the-art network architecture is actually derived or was actually selected by what the hardware can run well versus what is actually the best architecture
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: A shared instruction set is what makes small custom silicon affordable to build: with a common ISA the designer inherits the compiler, the opcodes and the operating system layer instead of writing a language and toolchain alongside the hardware, which frees effort for unusual accelerators built beside the core.
claims.quote_verbatim: because of the common ISA, it's like, okay, I don't have to write. I don't also have to write my whole coding language, you know, like all the op codes, all the language stuff, all that OS stuff
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: The accumulator register found in processor architectures descends from mechanical calculators. Adding a separate mechanical register that held a running result, instead of operating directly on the input mechanism, is what first made multiplication and division possible on those machines.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have a separate mechanical register called the accumulator, you can do more than you could do with a direct input scheme because you can actually all of a sudden do multiplication and division. And, you know, once you find that out, you, you, it actually clicks. Okay. So this is why, you know, if you look at a CPU, it has an accumulator register
claims.speaker: Michal Zalewski
claims.episode_title: The Secret Life of Circuits with lcamtuf / Michał Zalewski

attribution_notes: Episode 258 (Audeme): attribution_reliable is false on both passages, and the episode has two guests (Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland) whose turns are interleaved in the fused text. The content is unambiguously a guest describing their own product, but which guest is unsettled, so speaker is null on both claims.

Episode 325: both passages are labelled Chris Gammell, but the material claimed here is the guest's answer describing his own camera design ('We provide system solutions', the GPMC register bus into his FPGA). Reattributed to David Kronstein.

Episode 346 (Joe FitzPatrick): attribution_reliable is false on both passages, but the content is the guest narrating his own hardware-implant and PLC-JTAG research in the first person. Joe Fitzpatrick retained.

Episode 230: the passage describing the second graphics card, the overclocked i7 and the render comparison is labelled Chris Gammell, but it is the same first-person account that continues in the adjacent passage labelled Dave Jones ('going back to using my CPU'). Both claims attributed to Dave Jones. The market speculation later in the same passage ('Intel ... running out of market') is the other host's and was not extracted.

Episode 469: passages are labelled Chris Gammell, but the VexRiscv generator explanation and the 2D acceleration engine ('the one I had running at supercon was...') are the guest's own work. Reattributed to Craig J Bishop.

Episode 498 (Andrea Morello): attribution_reliable is false; the retained claim is the guest's own reply ('I'll respond to this by saying'), so Andrea Morello is retained. The interjected host line about ASICs was not extracted.
Episode 103: the passage about vendor IP portfolios and datasheet feature checklists is fused host/guest dialogue that could not be split cleanly, and was not extracted.

Episode 169: the reported 8051 soft-core clock rate and the '300 companies' clone count are stated once and inconsistently with the surrounding narration; the clone claim is written as 'hundreds of companies' and the clock figure is not asserted.
Episode 230: the processor part number is garbled in the transcript ('Intel i7, 377 OK'), so only the approximate clock rate is asserted.
